text: This capstone's lab, report, and case study pulled on every chapter of this course, not just the ones that sound like capstone material. This lesson traces each decision back to the chapter that made it possible, then closes the course and points to what's next.

Chapter 1's signed Rules of Engagement and scope are why Lesson 29 never paused to justify itself, and Chapter 2's attack surface map is why three hosts turned into three clear follow-up questions. Chapter 3's scanning and prioritization picked one host over two others, and Chapter 4's when-not-to-exploit judgment is exactly why check ran before exploit. Chapter 5's web testing discipline would apply identically to any other vulnerability class, Chapter 6's post-exploitation habits captured evidence the instant access was gained, and Chapter 7's purple team thinking is why this engagement felt complete rather than one-sided.

Strung together, the engagement runs as one continuous pipeline: authorization and recon, scanning and validated exploitation, immediate evidence capture, a professional CVSS-backed report, and a disciplined escalation when a finding turned out to be politically inconvenient. Methodology, tooling, and professional conduct aren't three separate skills here -- they're one skill, proven start to finish.

Ethical Hacking, Penetration Testing & Purple Team Operations is course 13 of the Cybersecurity Analyst to Security Engineer path, and one of four Expert Specialization courses: Digital Forensics & Malware Analysis, this one, AI Security Engineering & Adversarial AI Defense, and Enterprise Security Architecture, GRC & Risk Management. All four build on the Advanced Specialization stage but not on each other, so they can be taken in any order from here.

This course is done: eight chapters of methodology, recon, scanning, exploitation, web testing, post-exploitation, purple team operations, and a full capstone engagement from recon through a real report and an ethical escalation. Three independent Expert Specialization courses remain, and whichever one fits where you want to go next -- forensics, AI security, or architecture and governance -- is the right one to take.
